series: Climate Fiscal Policy Briefs, Section 3: Sovereign Incentives
title: Reward Governments, Not Projects

slides.title: Reward Governments, Not Projects
slides.subtitle: International incentives for national climate policy: Briefs 3.1–3.3
slides.message: Cash on the needed scale is politically impossible. Reward governments with what the international system supplies cheaply and they value highly: cheaper borrowing, through guarantees and collateral. Each dollar donors hold then delivers several dollars of incentive.

slides.title: Incentives must come from outside; cash fails

stats.label: a year to pay $100/t for cutting a tenth of global fossil CO₂ (about 3.7 Gt)
a year moved out of China alone by a $100/t global carbon tax
of incentive per donor dollar from cash, spent once

slides.text: A government that cuts emissions pays the whole cost and gets a small share of the benefit, so the reward must come from outside. Donors will not vote for cash on this scale, and payments against counterfactual baselines reward delay.

slides.title: Four routes to an incentive
rows: Payment per tonne cut by a policy, as a carbon-price equivalent
An intermediary and guarantees for its clean power pipeline, on condition of reform
A lower interest rate if agreed indicators are met
Notional capitalized value, backed by the Trust
A balance credited for carbon stocks, usable as guarantee capacity
Expected loss and buffer carry, held not paid out
slides.note: Policy crediting is the cleanest and dearest; de-risking is cheap but small. Section 3 aims for both size and low cost.

slides.title: A guarantee is worth more than it costs
slides.caption: Ratio of interest savings to the guarantor's expected loss, for three spread savings.
points: The borrower saves the full spread; the guarantor bears only expected loss.
Base case: 3% calls a year × 37% loss = 1.11% a year.
At a 3-point spread: 2.7 dollars per dollar; 10 at a 10% loss; about 80 on the MDB record.
Gabon's insured 2023 bond: 6.1%, against 9–10.5% on its other bonds.

left.heading: Definition
points: Opened by the verified carbon stock at a low stock price.
Debited at a uniform debit price per tonne above an allowance; credited below.
Never paid out: it sets guarantee capacity on green borrowing.
Two prices: Guyana's stock at $100/t is $1.95tn, which never binds.

right.heading: Worked example (stylized forest country)
points: $5bn balance, $50 debit, 15 Mt a year against an allowance falling to zero in 2050.
Saves $150m a year; business as usual exhausts the balance by 2042.
Each tonne costs the country about $30; acting is worth about $1bn.
Donors hold a $0.47bn buffer and expect to lose about $56m a year.

slides.title: The Climate Investment Trust: hold, don't spend
slides.caption: A: interest savings per donor dollar. B: Trust capital over 25 years from $5bn at launch (stylized, 3.2).
points: A 9.3% buffer keeps exhaustion to 1% a year, so $5bn supports about $54bn of guarantees.
They save borrowers $1.6bn a year. Paid as cash, that would exhaust $5bn in about three years.
Growth needs fees: about 0.8% a year on exposure to hold steady; $2.4bn a year from co-investment.

slides.title: Sustainability-linked lending is too small
slides.caption: Present value at 5% over ten years, US$ million, log scale. Hatched: cost to the funder.
points: Uruguay's $350m loan (2023) can save at most $12.5m, about $8m in present value.
A 100 bp step-down on $1bn: $77m. The stylized reform costs $770m.
$3.3bn of capacity is worth $772m; the funder expects to lose $286m.
Codify the loan and use it to deliver capacity.

slides.title: Paying for acting now
slides.caption: Net present value of adopting a stylized $1bn reform, by year of adoption.
points: Falling technology costs and the option to wait reward delay.
Minimum incentive to act now: $20/t; about $30 allowing for the value of waiting.
Capacity declining as technology costs fall halves donor cost: $740m to $370m. Cash: $1bn.
Forests need a permanent floor.

slides.title: How series 2 and 3 compose

left.heading: Section 2: who bears a loss
points: A payment intermediary and its guarantee waterfall (2.1).
Two-stage finance, pools and synthetic sovereign bonds (2.2).
Takes policy as given, and prices or conditions it.

right.heading: Section 3: what the government chooses
points: Capacity earned under 3.1 can stand in 2.1's waterfall or behind 2.2's senior bonds.
The Trust's regional funds hold 2.2's first-loss tranche.
One verified indicator can trigger both a rebate and capacity.

slides.text: A risk mechanism fails when the guarantor cannot pay; an incentive fails when the reward is too small, too late or in the wrong form.

slides.title: What to do
todo: MDB shareholders: rules-based guarantee capacity outside country envelopes, allocated by notional capitalized value.
Donors: fund the buffer, not the reward, in a Trust launched as insurance first.
MDBs: publish an indicator menu, baselines and pricing for sustainability-linked loans.
Make capacity the main prize, declining as clean technology gets cheaper.
Forest and coal countries: negotiate allowances, not baselines.
